chapter: Early listening, piano and adolescent conflict
title: Classical violin and piano lessons, the ruler on his hands
summary: His ear came from classical training; he learned piano from his mother and the Williams books, and a teacher hit his hands with a ruler.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Then you -- but you spoke specifically of jazz. Now when you first have been exposed to jazz? I mean you were exposed to it through the Mills Brothers, certainly, but where else?
Well, I didn't consider the Mills Brothers to be exactly jazz, although -- yes, I would have to consider in the field of jazz, yes. But now --

Yes. But in that order, as I said, my musical ear was trained from the classical music that I'd played in the citywide orchestra. Now, you must remember that I started out as a classical violinist, and I didn't study the piano formally as a classical pianist. I studied the piano by way of my mother teaching me the fundamentals, and I had a few lessons to teach me the fingerings. And I remember at that time I had been through the first three books of the Williams Piano Book, which included the Minuet in G, the last classical piece I remember being interested in or disgusted with because of the technicalities of the fingering.

And the teacher hit my hands with a ruler to make me realize that I didn't have them in the proper position, and my rebellion against being feminine type, as I said, because I was an athlete, you see, it didn't fit

me exactly. I was discouraged along the lines of classical music. As I said, along with the fact that many of these ruffians used to grab the violin and there was always the danger of it getting destroyed, or my being called a sissy.
